title: Vesak
hookLine: the May full moon: in Theravada lands, birth, awakening and passing remembered on one day

lines: A BIRTHDAY, A GRADUATION, A FUNERAL.
cards: A birthday, a graduation and a funeral, all on the same day. Every year. With lanterns.
That's roughly what the full moon of May holds across Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, and in Buddhist communities worldwide. Streets fill with lights. Temples fill up.
People dressed in white carry flowers and candles. It's a great holy day in these countries, and it holds three moments of one life at once.

teach.b: Vesak. The name comes from Vesakha, the month in the old Indian calendar that usually falls in April or May. In Theravada tradition, three events in the Buddha's life are remembered on its full moon.
His birth, in the garden at Lumbini.
His awakening, under the tree at Bodh Gaya.
And his passing into final nibbana, at Kusinara, eighty years later.

Born, awake, gone: one life, one night. The awakening is remembered with a Dhammapada verse tradition places on the Buddha's lips that night, addressed to craving as the builder of the house of the self.
In Max Muller's translation: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again."
His passing is remembered with his last words, from the long discourse on the final nibbana. In T. W.
Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" So one night holds a baby's first breath and an old man's last.
Tradition doesn't treat that as an accident of the calendar. It reads like the teaching itself: things arise, things pass, and in between, a person can wake up.
In 1950 the World Fellowship of Buddhists, a gathering from many countries, agreed to keep Vesak together, and in 1999 the United Nations recognized it too.

Other Buddhist traditions keep these events on separate days; you'll meet one tomorrow. Because it follows the moon, the date moves: some years it falls in June. And the lamp people light that night isn't for one moment.

how: On Vesak, Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing: many dress in white, visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food and light lanterns and lamps.

games.q: the Buddha is dying at Kusinara, and the monks are gathered. what are his last words, in the tradition's telling?
o: a new rule for the monks.
all things decay; keep going with diligence.
games.why: Rhys Davids translates them: 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!'

practice: Hold three moments of one life in mind, slowly: a baby's first breath in a garden, a man under a tree at dawn seeing clearly, an old man lying between two trees saying, keep going, with care.
Then feel your own breath; it began once, and it will end once. Right now, in between, it's here, so rest in this one.

wordCard.voice: Vesak. The full moon of Vesakha, when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on one day.

orig.note: Pali: the month of Vesakha (Sanskrit Vaishakha), which gives Vesak its name.

carryVoice: Your line: born, awake, gone. A baby's first breath and an old man's last, on one full moon. That's day one hundred forty-five.
